summary: Sets out requirements for DHCPv6 failover. DHCPv6 lets several servers share a network but gives them no way to share lease information, so redundancy is hard to do reliably. This document lists requirements, related problems and the proposed scope of a solution.

plainLanguage.summary: If two helpers hand out seats, they need to share a list, or both give away the same seat. This asks for a shared list.

questions: how to make dhcpv6 servers redundant
what are the dhcpv6 failover requirements
what is lease stability in dhcpv6
subtitle: What a standard way for two DHCPv6 servers to back each other up would have to do, and what it would leave out.

tldr.problem: DHCPv6 allows several servers on one network, but gives them no way to share which clients hold which leases, so reliable server redundancy is not possible.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys failover scenarios, failure modes and synchronization methods, then lists ten requirements for a future failover protocol built around exactly two partner servers.
tldr.outcome: It defines no protocol. It sets the requirements and scope that later design and protocol documents were expected to follow.

today: RFC 7031 is an Informational document published in September 2013, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines no protocol, only requirements and scope for later design and protocol documents.

sections.title: The Problem and the Scope of the Work
sections.content:
RFC 3315 lets several DHCPv6 servers operate on one network. It does not define how they share address and prefix pools, or how a client can extend its leases when the original server is down. For redundancy to work reliably, the cooperating primary and secondary servers must keep a consistent database of lease information.

This document does not define a DHCPv6 failover protocol. It gives background and a minimum set of requirements. The work is planned as documents of increasing specificity: this requirements document, then a design document, then, if there is enough interest, a protocol document. The idea borrows heavily from a DHCPv4 failover specification that never completed standardization but has several operationally proven vendor-specific implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Many servers can already hand out addresses, but they do not talk to each other. This paper is the first step toward making them share their notes.

sections.title: Simpler Alternatives to Failover
sections.content:
Often a simpler approach meets the goal, and the RFC lists four.

  • Short-lived addresses: for something like PXE network boot, give two or more servers distinct preference values (for example 10 and 20). The client picks the larger value, and if that server fails the next one keeps answering. The cost is no lease stability: clients' addresses and prefixes change on failure.
  • Redundant servers: simply run two or more independent servers on the same link, as discussed in RFC 6853.
  • Distributed databases: point two servers at one shared database. This only moves the single point of failure unless the database is itself reliable, and a network partition can still lead both servers to give the same address to different clients.
  • Load balancing: administrators who only want to share client traffic are advised to use a separate load-balancing mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you do not need a fancy plan. Two separate helpers, or a first-choice and a second-choice helper, can be enough.

sections.title: Failover Scenarios and Principles
sections.content:
The RFC describes deployment scenarios that people call failover. In the hot standby model one partner serves clients and the other takes over if it fails. Servers may also sit in distant data centers, share load, take part in several relationships (the 1-to-1, m-to-1 and m-to-n models), or split the pool into non-overlapping pieces.

It settles on a pair of servers. With more than two partners there would be intermediate, inconsistent states where some partners had an update and some did not, which would greatly complicate the protocol for little gain.

It also describes two failure modes. In a server failure the partner is simply down and recovery only needs a download of the healthy partner's lease database. In a network partition both servers may keep serving clients, so after the network rejoins they have two lease databases to reconcile, which is significantly more complicated. Partition is more likely when the servers are geographically far apart.
sections.plainLanguage: If a helper stops answering, maybe they went home, or maybe the hallway is blocked and they are still working. The hard part is telling these apart and fixing the lists afterward.

sections.title: Keeping the Lease Databases in Sync
sections.content:
Partners must exchange changes to the lease database. The RFC describes two methods.

With lockstep, a server that gets a REQUEST assigns the lease, sends it to its partner, waits for the partner's response and only then sends the REPLY to the client. The databases are always consistent, but every reply is delayed by two transmissions between partners plus the partner's write to permanent storage.

With lazy updates, the server sends the REPLY first and updates the partner later, or starts the update without waiting for a response. Response times barely change, but the databases are only loosely synchronized. If a server crashes after replying but before updating its partner, a client holds a lease the partner does not know about, which makes re-integration harder.
sections.plainLanguage: One helper can check with the other before telling you your seat, which is safe but slow. Or the helper can tell you right away and update the list afterward, which is fast but can go wrong if they trip in between.

sections.title: The Ten Requirements
sections.content:
The core protocol is expected to provide the following properties.

  • Exactly two partners know about a specific lease, and a server must not take part in more than one failover relationship for a given prefix or address pool.
  • The protocol must support the m-to-1 model, though an implementation may choose only 1-to-1.
  • One partner must be able to keep serving leases the other offered. This lease stability means a failure should have minimal or no impact on clients and must not force them to change addresses or delegated prefixes.
  • Prefix delegation must be supported.
  • Failover must not add significant delay to server responses, so synchronization must use some form of lazy updates.
  • The pair must recover from a server failure and from a network partition. Depending on the failure, recovery may need manual intervention.
  • The design must allow secure communication between the partners.
  • Extensions to the core protocol should be allowed when possible.

Explicitly out of scope are load balancing (an extension that must not be part of the core protocol), configuration synchronization, the m-to-n model, and servers in multiple relationships for the same pool.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules: exactly two helpers, you keep your seat if one leaves, it must stay fast, and the two must be able to fix their lists afterward.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The design must let each peer in a failover relationship identify the other, authenticate that identification, and validate that it is the intended peer. It should also optionally support confidentiality.

The eventual protocol specification should give operational guidelines for authentication mechanisms that depend on servers that might be unreachable, for example a remote Certificate Authority that cannot be reached during a network partition. Security for the design itself is left to the design document.
sections.plainLanguage: The two helpers must be sure they are really talking to each other and not to someone pretending.
